guide_text:
# Senior backend and AI systems interview preparation

A twelve-week program for senior backend or backend-leaning platform and product roles at AI companies. Distributed systems remains the spine. Version 6 keeps the hosted-inference, application-state, evaluation, recoverable-workflow, routing, and retrieval boundaries introduced in version 5, while replacing a generic WAL slot with reversible online migration, replacing basic hash sharding with quorum-safe leader/follower replication, and narrowing cache stampede work to expiration herds, request coalescing, and TTL jitter. It does not target research, model training infrastructure, GPU kernels, or inference-runtime implementation.

Each week remains exactly twenty dependable hours. Eleven existing Learn hours are reallocated to explicit AI application-systems work; the existing five hours of ChatGPT design practice bring the explicit AI total to sixteen hours without increasing the 240-hour plan. Primary technical sources now ground the changed Week 2 and Week 3 retrieval work, every coding exercise is implemented in Python, and full designs and mocks remain external performance evidence. Global Unprompted reviews remain separate from plan capacity and begin only after the mapped source lesson and reviewed card authority are complete.

An additional stretch menu offers up to twenty hours each week without blocking advancement or changing the forecast. Stretch work deepens the current week through unseen Python problems, additional designs, case studies, behavioral rehearsal, and sourced gap repair; it never pre-teaches the next week or creates generic card volume. Resume work, job applications, and professional networking are intentionally deferred.
title: Senior backend and AI systems interview preparation
subject: Senior backend and AI systems interview preparation

phases.description: Build the delivery method, hosted-inference boundaries, data foundations, and coding patterns that later designs depend on.
Apply scaling, resilience, bounded AI workflow, realtime, and storage patterns in complete designs.
Choose concrete data, messaging, retrieval, stream, gateway, and coordination systems from their mechanics.
Convert knowledge into repeatable performance through named mocks and focused repair.

items.title: Learn the system design delivery framework
items.why: A stable sequence prevents premature deep dives and gets a complete design on the board.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson, write the sequence from memory, and speak one ten-minute requirements-to-deep-dives walkthrough without notes.
mapped_recall_topics: System design delivery: requirements to entities, APIs, high-level design, and deep dives
Non-functional requirements: turning scale, latency, availability, and durability into design constraints
Decision-driven estimation: calculating only the bound that can change an architectural choice

stretch_actions.title: Solve additional unseen Week 1 Python problems
stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight additional problems from the same three families and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.title: Complete two additional delivery-framework designs
stretch_actions.done_when: Run two blind designs and compare each with a trusted breakdown.

stretch_actions.title: Deepen one current-week source or case study
stretch_actions.done_when: Study one source and write the decision, trade-off, and failure it clarifies.

stretch_actions.title: Rehearse one evidence-backed behavioral story
stretch_actions.done_when: Draft, speak, and revise one story with individual actions and a measurable result.

stretch_actions.title: Harvest stretch-session gaps
stretch_actions.done_when: Record the stretch gaps and add no more than three source-grounded recall prompts.

items.title: Design APIs with trusted identity and stable pagination
items.why: Identity and traversal mistakes turn otherwise sound backend designs into security or correctness failures.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and draft one resource API that derives the caller from trusted context and pages a changing collection with a stable cursor.
mapped_recall_topics: API identity boundary: deriving the principal from trusted authentication context before authorizing a resource or action
Cursor pagination: preserving stable traversal while new rows are inserted

items.title: Trace hosted LLM inference and make ambiguous retries safe
items.why: Hosted inference is probabilistic, token-by-token remote computation; a timeout still cannot prove whether provider work or an adjacent write happened, so retry and idempotency semantics must be explicit.
items.done_when: Read all three sources, then draw one Devmax-style request from prompt assembly and tokenization through prefill, decode, streaming, structured output, timeout, retry, and reconciliation; distinguish training from inference and state which effect owns the idempotency key.
mapped_recall_topics: Timeouts, retries, and idempotency across a partial network failure
Training versus hosted inference: parameter updates versus prediction with a deployed model
Hosted LLM request lifecycle: tokenization, prefill, autoregressive decode, and latency boundaries

items.title: Implement two-pointer invariants in Python
items.why: Two-pointer interviews depend on proving why one pointer can move without discarding the answer.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and state the movement invariant, time complexity, and one failure mode without notes.

items.title: Implement sliding-window state in Python
items.why: Sliding-window problems test whether changing state can be updated without rescanning the whole range.
items.done_when: Study the lesson, solve both problems in Python, and explain the validity condition, expansion, contraction, and complexity without notes.

items.title: Implement interval sweeps in Python
items.why: Interval questions test ordering, boundary semantics, and whether one active range summarizes processed work.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and explain sorting, the active boundary, overlap semantics, and complexity without notes.

items.title: Design Bitly blind before opening the breakdown
items.why: A simple product exposes delivery discipline without hiding behind advanced infrastructure.
items.done_when: Spend 15 minutes scoping, 45 minutes designing blind, then open the breakdown, compare for 90 minutes, redraw for 60 minutes, and record three concrete differences in the final 30 minutes.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 1 gap
items.why: Observed failures should outrank generic catalog breadth.
items.done_when: Debrief the Bitly and Python work, name the highest-impact gap, repair it from a cited source, and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Build a behavioral evidence inventory
items.why: Strong behavioral answers begin with real evidence, not polished generic scripts.
items.done_when: Create eight rows for scope, ownership, ambiguity, perseverance, conflict, growth, communication, and leadership, each tied to one real event or explicitly marked missing.

items.title: Reconstruct Week 1 decisions closed-book
items.why: Retrieval distinguishes usable knowledge from recognition immediately after study.
items.done_when: Without notes, reconstruct the delivery sequence, one API trust boundary, one retry path, and the recognition cue for each coding family; record every miss.

weeks.full_title: Data models, indexes, and AI application state

items.title: Model prompts, conversations, and eval evidence from access patterns
items.why: A model has a context window, not durable application memory; prompt versions, turns, outputs, provenance, permissions, and eval labels need a schema derived from the product's reads and writes.
items.done_when: For five queries (resume a conversation, reproduce a score, compare prompt versions, audit answer authority, and inspect an eval result), derive entities, relationships, read paths, write paths, and one justified denormalization; label model weights, request context, durable application state, and code-owned policy separately.
mapped_recall_topics: Data modeling from access patterns: deriving entities, relationships, and query shapes
Denormalization: duplicating data for a read path without losing update correctness
Context windows versus durable conversation state: explicit history, storage, retention, and compaction

stretch_actions.title: Solve additional unseen Week 2 Python problems
stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight additional current-week problems and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.title: Complete two additional data-heavy designs
stretch_actions.done_when: Run two blind designs and compare each with a trusted breakdown.

stretch_actions.title: Deepen one Week 2 database question
stretch_actions.done_when: Study one current-week source and write the mechanism, trade-off, and failure it resolves.

stretch_actions.title: Rehearse scope and ownership follow-ups

stretch_actions.title: Harvest stretch-session gaps

items.title: Choose indexes from query shape
items.why: Indexes help only when their ordering and coverage match the actual access path.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and choose one single-column and one composite index, explaining ordering, coverage, and write cost.
mapped_recall_topics: B-tree lookup and range scans: how page locality shapes read cost
Composite indexes: left-prefix matching, column order, and covering a query

items.title: Migrate live data and reason about concurrent snapshots
items.why: Senior backend work requires both reversible live-schema changes and an exact account of what concurrent transactions can see and safely update.
items.done_when: Read both sources, then write one no-downtime migration sequence from dual write through retirement and trace one Repeatable Read conflict through full-transaction retry.
mapped_recall_topics: Online data migration: dual writing, backfill, compare, cutover, and rollback
MVCC snapshots: letting readers and writers proceed while isolation anomalies remain bounded

items.title: Implement stack state in Python
items.why: Stacks encode unresolved work and nested structure with explicit state.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and state what each stack entry means at every step.

items.title: Implement linked-list pointer changes in Python
items.why: Pointer updates test whether state can change without losing the remaining structure.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and narrate each pointer update before executing it.

items.title: Implement binary-search boundaries in Python
items.why: Binary search succeeds only when the retained half and termination condition are proved.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and state the search invariant and boundary convention before coding.

items.title: Design LeetCode blind before opening the breakdown
items.why: The prompt connects APIs, submission state, access patterns, and indexes in one backend system.
items.done_when: Complete a 45-minute blind design, compare it with the breakdown, redraw the data and request paths, and name three changed decisions.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 2 gap
items.why: Data-access mistakes compound in every later design.
items.done_when: Debrief the week, repair one observed mechanism from its cited lesson, and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Develop scope and ownership evidence
items.why: Senior behavioral signal depends on individual decisions and consequences.
items.done_when: Choose one scope and one ownership example, write the situation, your individual decisions, measurable result, and likely follow-up questions.

items.title: Reconstruct Week 2 data decisions closed-book
items.why: Closed-book reconstruction exposes whether storage vocabulary is connected to actual query behavior.
items.done_when: Derive a model and index set for a fresh prompt, trace one commit and snapshot, and identify all three coding patterns without notes.

items.title: Design cache-aside paths and contain expiration herds
items.why: Caching improves latency only when miss population, write invalidation, synchronized expiry, and same-key refill behavior are explicit.
items.done_when: Read both sources, trace one hit/miss/update race, then explain how TTL jitter spreads cross-key expiry while single-flight refill suppresses same-key concurrency.
mapped_recall_topics: Cache-aside reads: miss handling, population, invalidation, and stale-data windows
Cache stampede: expiration herds, request coalescing, and TTL jitter

stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight current-week problems and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.title: Harvest stretch-session gaps
stretch_actions.done_when: Record gaps and add no more than three source-grounded recall prompts.

items.title: Partition, rebalance, replicate, and choose partition behavior
items.why: Partition ownership and replication together determine routing, movement during growth, ordered scans, acknowledged-write safety, and behavior during a network partition.
items.done_when: Read all four sources, then trace one ordered-tablet split including client routing, one virtual-node join, and one majority-committed leader failover before assigning operation-specific behavior during a partition.
mapped_recall_topics: Leader/follower replication: majority commit, lagging followers, and safe failover
Range sharding: ordered tablets, split boundaries, and scan-preserving routing
Consistent hashing: ring ownership, virtual nodes, and bounded key movement
CAP during a partition: choosing which operations remain available and which must reject

items.title: Implement heap selection in Python
items.why: Heap problems test whether only candidates that can still affect the answer are retained.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and justify heap contents, size, and complexity.

items.title: Implement depth-first search in Python
items.why: DFS requires precise recursive state, visited ownership, and return meaning.
items.done_when: Study the lesson, solve both problems in Python, and state the frame state and return value before coding.

items.title: Implement breadth-first search in Python
items.why: BFS derives shortest unweighted distance and level order from queue discipline.
items.done_when: Study the lesson, solve both problems in Python, and explain enqueue-time visitation and level boundaries.

items.title: Design a distributed cache blind
items.why: The prompt forces routing, replication, consistency, hot-key, and failure decisions to work together.
items.done_when: Complete a 45-minute blind design, compare with the breakdown, redraw it, and defend partitioning plus failure behavior.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 3 gap
items.why: Caching and partition gaps propagate into every later architecture.
items.done_when: Repair one observed gap from a cited source and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Develop ambiguity and perseverance evidence
items.why: Senior signal includes making progress when facts or resources are incomplete.
items.done_when: Draft one ambiguity and one perseverance example with the uncertainty, your decision, result, and learning.

items.title: Reconstruct Week 3 trade-offs closed-book
items.why: Retrieval verifies that partition and cache vocabulary can drive a fresh decision.
items.done_when: Design the routing and cache path for a fresh scenario, choose partition behavior, and identify all three coding families without notes.

weeks.full_title: Scaling, fan-out, and measured AI reliability

items.title: Scale reads, replicas, and feed fan-out
items.why: Read paths need different materialization and consistency choices under skew.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson, study the historical Twitter case, and compare read-time, write-time, and hybrid feed materialization including replica lag.
mapped_recall_topics: Scaling reads: composing caches, read replicas, and denormalized views
Replica lag: preserving read-your-writes and monotonic reads after a write
Fan-out mechanics: choosing write-time materialization or read-time aggregation

stretch_actions.title: Solve additional unseen graph problems in Python
stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight current-week problems and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.title: Complete two additional scaling designs
stretch_actions.done_when: Run two blind designs and compare each with a trusted breakdown.

stretch_actions.title: Deepen the historical Twitter case
stretch_actions.done_when: Study the case and write three architectural constraints and their consequences.

stretch_actions.title: Rehearse conflict and growth follow-ups
stretch_actions.done_when: Speak both examples and answer at least five probes.

stretch_actions.title: Harvest stretch-session gaps
stretch_actions.done_when: Record gaps and add no more than three source-grounded recall prompts.

items.title: Scale writes and contain overload
items.why: Write systems fail when skew and backlog grow faster than bounded consumers can absorb.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and trace partitioning, batching, backpressure, and load shedding through one burst scenario.
mapped_recall_topics: Scaling writes: partitioning, batching, and asynchronous ingestion under skew
Backpressure and load shedding: keeping overload from becoming a cascading failure

items.title: Operate bounded inference workers and measure reliability
items.why: AI queues move expensive, variable-duration work; concurrency, token budgets, retries, poison inputs, and semantic evals determine whether overload becomes a bill, an outage, or a silent product regression.
items.done_when: For one scoring workload, write a one-page worker contract covering admission, concurrency and token budgets, ordering requirements, per-item idempotency, retry limits, dead-letter handling, and queue-age plus model-latency metrics; then run four labelled cases from the committed eval pack, repeat one failure-sensitive case three times, and report schema pass, semantic pass, and failure classes separately.
mapped_recall_topics: Queue workers: controlling concurrency, ordering, retries, and dead-letter handling
Evaluation-driven reliability: realistic cases, repeated trials, calibrated graders, and regression gates

items.title: Implement graph dependency ordering in Python
items.why: Dependency problems require converting constraints into an explicit processing frontier.
items.done_when: Study topological sorting, solve both problems in Python, and explain indegrees, cycle detection, and complexity.

items.title: Implement shortest paths in Python
items.why: Shortest-path interviews test when a distance becomes final and how edge assumptions change the algorithm.
items.done_when: Study the lesson, solve both problems in Python, and justify the frontier, relaxation rule, and complexity.

items.title: Design a Twitter-style home timeline blind
items.why: Power-user skew forces a hybrid rather than one-size-fits-all fan-out decision.
items.done_when: Design blind for 45 minutes before opening the breakdown; then explain ordinary-account materialization, high-follower merging, lag, ordering, and overload.

items.title: Design an ad-click aggregator
items.why: A write-heavy pipeline makes batching, partitions, backpressure, and late processing observable.
items.done_when: Run a timed design, compare it with the breakdown, and revise the ingestion and aggregation paths around one overload failure.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 4 gap
items.why: Scaling depth should follow observed bottlenecks.
items.done_when: Repair one observed gap from a cited source and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Develop conflict and growth evidence
items.why: Senior behavior includes productive disagreement and changed future behavior.
items.done_when: Draft one conflict and one growth example with your choice, other perspectives, result, and learning.

items.title: Reconstruct scaling decisions closed-book
items.why: Retrieval tests whether skew and failure can drive architecture without a memorized feed diagram.
items.done_when: Reconstruct both designs, state the fan-out split, and identify graph versus shortest-path cues without notes.

weeks.full_title: Contention, bounded AI workflows, and resilience

items.title: Protect invariants under contention
items.why: The right concurrency control follows the invariant and failure model, not a favorite lock.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and choose among a conditional write, pessimistic lock, OCC, serializable transaction, and lease for two scenarios.
mapped_recall_topics: Contention control: choosing a conditional write, pessimistic lock, OCC, or serializable isolation for one invariant
Distributed locks: leases, TTL expiry, fencing tokens, and stale owners

stretch_actions.title: Solve additional unseen Week 5 Python problems
stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight current-week problems and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.title: Complete two additional workflow designs
stretch_actions.done_when: Run two blind designs and compare each with a trusted breakdown.

stretch_actions.title: Deepen one contention or workflow mechanism
stretch_actions.done_when: Study one source and write the invariant, trade-off, and failure it resolves.

stretch_actions.title: Rehearse communication and leadership follow-ups
stretch_actions.done_when: Speak both examples and answer at least five probes.

stretch_actions.title: Harvest stretch-session gaps
stretch_actions.done_when: Record gaps and add no more than three source-grounded recall prompts.

items.title: Bound tool authority in recoverable AI workflows
items.why: Model output is nondeterministic and provider calls can fail after money or state changed; durable progress, least-privilege tools, validation, deduplication, and code-owned stop rules must define what may be retried or committed.
items.done_when: Draw a persisted, resumable state machine for one score-or-import workflow from prompt version and provider call through schema and semantic validation, database commit, and downstream effect. Mark deterministic code versus bounded model decisions, least-privilege tool scopes, attempt or token budgets, and stop or approval conditions; then inject a timeout, invalid JSON, unsupported claim, unauthorized tool proposal, crash, and duplicate delivery and show the retry, compensation, containment, idempotent resume, or stop decision for each.
mapped_recall_topics: Saga compensation: recovering a partially completed multi-service workflow
Durable workflow orchestration: persisting progress across retries, crashes, and long waits
Circuit breakers, bulkheads, and jittered retries: containing a dependency failure
Exactly-once effects: combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication and idempotency

items.title: Implement backtracking in Python
items.why: Backtracking correctness depends on precise choose, recurse, undo, and pruning behavior.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and narrate the search state and undo step.

items.title: Implement dynamic programming in Python
items.why: DP tests whether state, transition, base cases, and evaluation order form one complete recurrence.
items.done_when: Study the fundamentals, solve both problems in Python, and implement one solution both top-down and bottom-up.

items.title: Implement greedy choices in Python
items.why: A greedy answer is credible only when the local choice cannot damage the global optimum.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and give an exchange argument or counterexample to a tempting alternative.

items.title: Design Ticketmaster under contention
items.why: Seat inventory exposes the difference between protecting an invariant and merely retrying conflicts.
items.done_when: Complete a blind design before the breakdown, then revise reservation, expiry, purchase, and oversell failure paths.

items.title: Design a payment workflow
items.why: Payments make partial completion, idempotency, reconciliation, and auditability non-negotiable.
items.done_when: Run a timed design, compare with the breakdown, and repair one ambiguous or partially completed transaction path.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 5 gap
items.why: Workflow reliability improves by repairing a concrete failed path.
items.done_when: Repair one observed gap from a cited source and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Develop communication and leadership evidence
items.why: Senior scope includes aligning people and improving outcomes without relying on authority.
items.done_when: Choose one communication and one leadership example and outline your decision, influence, result, and learning.

items.title: Reconstruct resilience decisions closed-book
items.why: Retrieval tests whether invariants and partial failures drive the mechanism choice.
items.done_when: Reconstruct both designs, choose contention and workflow mechanisms, and identify all three coding families without notes.

weeks.full_title: Realtime delivery, blobs, and durable AI jobs

items.title: Choose realtime delivery and reconnect recovery
items.why: Persistent delivery requires both protocol choice and recovery after the connection inevitably breaks.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and compare polling, long polling, SSE, and WebSockets, then design heartbeats, missed-event cursors, and backfill.
mapped_recall_topics: Real-time delivery: server polling, long-polling, SSE, and WebSocket connection state
Reconnect recovery: heartbeats, sticky routing, missed-event cursors, and backfill

stretch_actions.done_when: Complete up to eight current-week problems and postmortem every miss.

stretch_actions.done_when: Run two blind designs and compare each with a trusted breakdown.

stretch_actions.done_when: Record gaps and add no more than three source-grounded recall prompts.

items.title: Upload, process, and deliver large blobs
items.why: Large payloads need resumability and object-storage paths that avoid application-server bottlenecks.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson and trace presigned multipart upload, integrity checking, asynchronous processing, origin storage, and delivery.
mapped_recall_topics: Large-object upload: presigned URLs, multipart chunks, checksums, and resumability
Large-blob delivery: resumable upload, asynchronous processing, object storage, and CDN origin

items.title: Expose durable state for long-running AI jobs
items.why: Large imports and batch inference outlive a request; accepted, running, failed, canceled, and completed must remain durable while publication cannot drift from the committed result.
items.done_when: Design a guide-import or batch-inference API with a submission token, pollable status, cancellation boundary, retry semantics, result retention, and webhook or outbox publication; state what the client sees after a crash before the provider call, after provider success, and after the database commit.
mapped_recall_topics: Transactional outbox: atomically committing business data before reliable publication
Long-running jobs: submission tokens, status polling, cancellation, and webhook completion

items.title: Implement tries in Python
items.why: Tries make shared prefix state and traversal costs explicit.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and explain node state, branching, terminal markers, and complexity.

items.title: Implement prefix sums in Python
items.why: Prefix state turns repeated range work into constant-time differences or frequency lookups.
items.done_when: Study the overview, solve both problems in Python, and define exactly what each prefix entry contains.

items.title: Implement matrix traversal in Python
items.why: Matrix questions test coordinate transforms, boundaries, and preservation of unread state.
items.done_when: Study the lesson, solve both problems in Python, and state boundary changes before each traversal or rotation.

items.title: Design WhatsApp realtime delivery
items.why: Messaging combines connection state, ordering, offline recovery, and durable delivery.
items.done_when: Complete a blind design before the breakdown, then revise connection, message, acknowledgement, and reconnect paths.

items.title: Design Dropbox blob processing
items.why: File synchronization connects resumable blobs, metadata, background processing, and conflict behavior.
items.done_when: Run a timed design, compare with the breakdown, and repair upload, change propagation, and interrupted-work paths.

items.title: Repair the highest-impact Week 6 gap
items.why: Realtime and long-running failures are best learned from the path that actually broke.
items.done_when: Repair one observed gap from a cited source and propose no more than three focused recall cards.

items.title: Finish the story catalog and draft the Big Three
items.why: A complete evidence pool makes common prompts specific instead of generic.
items.done_when: Fill every missing evidence row and draft tell-me-about-yourself, proud-project, and conflict answers using real examples.

items.title: Reconstruct realtime and job recovery closed-book
items.why: Retrieval verifies that connection and job recovery are understood beyond protocol names.
items.done_when: Reconstruct both designs, trace one reconnect and crash, and identify all three coding families without notes.

items.done_when: Finish the lesson and defend PostgreSQL for one workload while naming the first write or scale limit that changes the choice.

items.title: Choose Redis structures and failure behavior
items.why: Redis is useful only when the data structure, durability, and eviction behavior match the role.
items.done_when: Finish the lesson, choose structures for three access patterns, and trace one memory-pressure or restart failure.
mapped_recall_topics: Redis data structures: choosing strings, hashes, sorted sets, streams, and HyperLogLog by access pattern
Redis durability and eviction: reconstructing failure behavior under memory pressure

items.title: Model DynamoDB keys without hot partitions

items.why: An inference gateway can centralize trusted identity, consent, per-user spend, prompt policy, model routing, and audit metadata, but it also becomes a sensitive bottleneck and failure boundary.

items.title: Build permission-filtered retrieval for grounded generation
items.why: RAG quality starts with ingestion and retrieval: exact terms, freshness, chunking, permissions, and semantic similarity fail differently, and fluent generation cannot repair missing or unauthorized evidence.
items.done_when: Using the committed retrieval lab's ten-chunk, nine-document versioned corpus, inspect its document-version, chunk, provenance, and tenant or ACL metadata; trace one update through Elasticsearch refresh and merge, run three labelled queries through lexical and semantic or hybrid retrieval, record top-k evidence, and demonstrate that access filtering occurs before reranking and citation context reaches generation.

items.title: Tune vector retrieval and evaluate end-to-end RAG

dependencies.rationale: The blind design practices the delivery framework.
The design requires an API boundary.
The design must handle request failure.
The timeline design applies fan-out and read scaling.
The auction requires an explicit storage choice.
The auction may use cache structures deliberately.
The full design applies rate-limit mechanics.
The search design applies index mechanics.
The Uber design applies proximity indexing.
The baseline uses completed mock evidence.
Final repair follows the evidence review.
